pr_title: Use deferred evaluation in ReadOnlyDictionary.Key/Value collections.
pr_body: Fixes #93829. I think this approach offers the best of both worlds, giving correct results for collections that create new instances every time, while not substantially impacting performance for collections that cache their key and value collections.

> ```cs
> Console.WriteLine(rodKeys.Count); // 0. This is not a problem. We should not change it.
> Console.WriteLine(rod.Keys.Count); // 0. But this is unacceptable, which need to be fixed.
> ```

👍 

> ```cs
> if (_keys != null && _keys._collection == mKeys) return _keys;
> ```

Instead of `==` I would use `ReferenceEquals` here. Because of more readability and it is what you actually doing here.
Further because it guards you against someone's overload of `==` in its own `Dictionary.Keys` implementation.

> Is this PR waiting for approving or to have more commits?

It's pending the conversation in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/93870#discussion_r1368745090

> The fix could be something like:
> 
> ```cs
>     public KeyCollection Keys => new KeyCollection(m_dictionary.Keys);
> ```

This would be penalizing performance for ROD users not wrapping `ConcurrentDictionary`.

> or an optimization version:

The issue with that approach is that it doesn't fully address the issue of `_keys` rooting stale entries from `ConcurrentDictionary`.  It will keep stale data until the getter is re-evaluated, which may never happen.

issue_context.title: ReadOnlyDictionary Keys/Values property does not reflect changes if underlying Dictionary is a ConcurrentDictionary and was used one time before
comments: I've opened a PR that should address the issue: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/93870/

> However, `ConcurrentDictionary.Keys` returns a static copy: ([seems not documented](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.concurrent.concurrentdictionary-2.keys?view=net-7.0))
> 
> ```cs
> ConcurrentDictionary<string, string> cd = new();
> var ckeys = cd.Keys;
> cd.TryAdd("a", "");
> Console.WriteLine(ckeys.Count); // print 0
> ```
> 
> I don't think it's a bug. And the behavior is unlikely to be changed.

Yes, it seems not documented. In the case of [ConcurrentDictionary.Count](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.concurrent.concurrentdictionary-2.count?view=net-7.0) it is documented that it uses snapshot semantics.

It is also my opinion that the `ConcurrentDictionary` behaves correctly. The snapshot behavior (and also acquiring all locks) of `Keys`, `Values` and `Count` are also mentioned by some blog posts.

> Anyway, we should fix `ReadOnlyDictionary.Keys` for no guarantee that the underlying `IDictionary`'s `Keys` returns a dynamic collection.
> Similar situation on `Values`.

Yes, that seems to be the solution. But we should think about performance when using the returned `KeyCollection` for more than just iteration with one call to `GetEnumerator`. If so it would result in populating a new snapshot of the `ConcurrentDictionary` all the time. It should be rare that it is used more than that but we cannot know,

review_comments: This changes behavior for ConcurrentDictionary, e.g. every access will be against the live collection vs against a cache. Is that the goal?
Yes, effectively it favors paying the price of populating these collections every time rather than reporting inconsistent data.

But it'll now be inconsistent with ConcurrentDictionary.  If you get the keys collection from ConcurrentDictionary, you'll be getting a snapshot, but if you get it from a wrapping ReadOnlyDictionary, you'll be getting a non-snapshot.  It's definitely a breaking change.  If we're really considering taking such a breaking change, we should consider going all the way and changing CD rather than changing ROD, such that CD.Keys/Values have non-snapshot behavior.

> If you get the keys collection from ConcurrentDictionary, you'll be getting a snapshot, but if you get it from a wrapping ReadOnlyDictionary, you'll be getting a non-snapshot.

Is that an issue though? ReadOnlyDictionary is wrapping dictionaries, not their key/value collections. I think it's a bigger problem that ReadOnlyDictionary can be inconsistent w.r.t. its own key/value collections.
The getter of `ReadOnlyDictionary.Keys` returning a snapshot is not a problem. The only thing we need to fix is that now it can return an outdated snapshot.

With these changes working with `ReadOnlyDictionary.Keys` or `.Values` or in other words working with the `KeyCollection` or `ValueCollection` can degrade performance if populating a new snapshot of `ConcurrentDictionary.Keys`/`.Values` now.
For example if using `Count` of `KeyCollection`  and after that the Enumerator. There are two calls to `_dictionary.Keys` in that case resulting in two populated snapshots.

But as you  already said:

> [...] paying the price of populating these collections every time rather than reporting inconsistent data.

I do not have a better solution right now, so maybe this is the best you can do about it.

> might now blow up in situations it didn't use to, e.g. because the collection might be growing concurrently, but the cached snapshot prevents concurrency-related problems.

Wouldn't the same concern apply if we changed ConcurrentDictionary to use live collections rather than snapshots?

> Wouldn't the same concern apply if we changed ConcurrentDictionary to use live collections rather than snapshots?

Yes, which is why I said if we're really considering making a breaking change like this, we should consider instead making it in CD.  Either way, it's a non-trivial impact.

> You're changing from a cached snapshot to a new snapshot on every access. From a performance perspective, every access to ReadOnlyDictionary.Keys will now be copying the full collection rather than being ammortized allocation-free.

That's assuming the underlying dictionary uses snapshot semantics. One alternative approach might be to avoid caching the ROD collections altogether, which would make it more faithful to the underlying type:

```diff
-public KeyCollection Keys => _keys ??= new KeyCollection(m_dictionary.Keys);
+public KeyCollection Keys => new KeyCollection(m_dictionary.Keys);
```

However that would end up penalizing performance in collections that don't use snapshotting.

I'm growing increasingly convinced that the current behavior isn't great when used in conjunction with ConcurrentDictionary. It's not just that it reports stale data, the ROD also has the potential of rooting entries that have long been wiped from the underlying CD.

> I'm growing increasingly convinced that the current behavior isn't great when used in conjunction with ConcurrentDictionary.

I'm not disagreeing.  I'm saying this change to address those concerns has its own risks.
Yes, but if your concern is consistency within a type, as you've expressed for ROD, the snapshot behavior of Keys on CD has all the same issues (and is the root cause of the concerns with ROD).

It's not exactly the same though, because CD will return a fresh snapshot every time you get it but ROD will cache the first snapshot for its entire lifetime. I actually don't mind the snapshotting semantics of CD, in many cases it might actually be desirable (although I can see how it could trip users up).
